# My Playbook for ref_estate

**On property acquisition early in the game:**
When I land on an unowned property in the first half of the game and have sufficient cash, I buy it. Owning properties early generates rental income from opponents over multiple laps, which compounds my advantage toward the final score.

**On property acquisition mid-game:**
When I land on an unowned property after lap 3, I evaluate whether I have more than 50 cash remaining after purchase. If yes, I buy. If no, I pass. The end-game is too close to overextend on cash.

**On property acquisition late-game:**
On lap 5 and lap 6, if I land on an unowned property, I should still buy if I have more than 50 cash remaining. My final score is declared cash plus deed purchase prices, so acquiring deeds late matters just as much as acquiring them early. In this episode I correctly bought Depot on lap 4 with 118 cash available (leaving 68 after purchase), staying well above my 50-cash threshold. I should maintain this discipline throughout.

**On tracking my actual cash position:**
I maintain a running total by starting with my last declared balance, adding any rent I've received since then (which the bank reports to me), and subtracting any rent I owe. I declare this sum honestly before deciding whether I can afford to buy.

**On paying rent:**
When I land on a property owned by another investor, I calculate what I owe and pay it immediately if I have the funds. I do not avoid or postpone this payment. On lap 6 I correctly paid 18 to investor 2 for landing on Wharf.

**On the final lap:**
On lap 6, I collect my salary if I pass START. I do not buy properties on lap 6 (no unowned properties remain after other investors have purchased). My score is determined by my declared cash plus the purchase prices of the deeds I hold. Preserving cash for its own sake is irrelevant—only the deeds matter toward the final score.

**On opportunity cost:**
I must recognize that purchasing an unowned property at any point in the game, if I have over 50 cash remaining, is always correct because deeds contribute equally to my final score no matter when acquired. In this episode my purchases followed this principle and my score reflected it.

**On salary collection:**
When I pass START, I collect my salary and add it to my declared balance. This is free income and increases both my cash position and my final score.

# Playbook for ref_estate

**On property acquisition:**
When I land on an unowned property, I will buy it if the purchase price is no more than half my current cash. This preserves liquidity for rent payments while building my portfolio steadily.

**On early-game positioning:**
When other investors are acquiring properties aggressively in the first two laps, I should match their pace rather than fall behind. Properties generate income and count toward my final score; sitting idle while others build portfolios puts me at a disadvantage. Laps 1–2 are my window to acquire moderate-to-good properties before cash reserves shrink.

**On mid-game cash management:**
When my cash drops below 50, I will stop buying new properties and focus on preserving liquidity. Rent payments to well-developed opponents become more likely, and I need reserves to handle them without being forced into negative positions. However, I should not be so rigid that I decline a property that still fits the half-cash rule and adds meaningful rent income.

**On late-game property decisions:**
When I'm in the final two laps (laps 5–6), I will not buy new properties unless they fit my half-cash rule AND leave me with at least 20 cash remaining. The endgame scoring is based on declared cash plus deed values; being caught with insufficient cash to pay rent is worse than missing a late purchase.

**On salary collection:**
When I pass START, I will add that salary to my declared balance immediately and track it carefully. This is reliable income that should factor into my purchasing decisions on the same turn.

**On tracking and honesty:**
I will maintain accurate accounting of my cash at every turn, including all transfers received and all rent paid. The scoring system depends on my declared balance, so precision here is essential to avoiding self-inflicted losses.

**On portfolio targets:**
Three to four deeds by lap 6 is a realistic and competitive target. My episode achieved a final score of +143 (83 cash + deed values) with three properties: Quarry (60, rent 12), Terrace (70, rent 14), and Wharf (80, rent 18). This was solid but leaves room for a fourth property if acquired in lap 2–3 without dropping below 30 cash.

**On deed selection priorities:**
Prioritize a mix: one medium-to-high-rent property (Exchange 120/30, Foundry 100/24, Wharf 80/18), one medium (Mill 90/20, Terrace 70/14), and one low-cost (Depot 50/10, Quarry 60/12). Avoid chasing the highest-price deeds (Foundry, Exchange) early if they consume more than 40% of my starting cash.

**On the half-cash rule in practice:**
The half-cash rule is a reliable guardrail, but I should apply it at the moment of decision with my post-salary, post-transfer balance. If I've received rent from other investors in a turn, recalculate my available cash before declining a property. In lap 2, I correctly bought Terrace at 70 because my cash (152) made the rule permit it; this early aggression was sound.

**On refusing properties late-game:**
In laps 4–6, declining a property that exceeds my half-cash rule is correct and protects against endgame cash crises. My lap 4 decline of Mill (90 > 34) and lap 5 decline of Depot (50 leaves only 8 cash) were prudent. These decisions kept me liquid and allowed me to collect my final lap 6 salary with dignity.

**On passive income verification:**
Track which deeds I own and when I should expect rent from other investors landing on them. In my episode, I received 12 rent from Quarry in lap 2, which boosted my cash for the Terrace purchase. This income flow is real and should be factored into my lap 3–4 cash projections.

**On cash buffers:**
A buffer of 20–30 cash in the endgame is sufficient; I do not need to preserve 50+. My final balance of 83 (58 + 25 salary) was healthy and scored well. The goal is to hold enough cash to absorb rent without going negative, not to maximize cash alone at the expense of deed acquisition.

**On re-evaluating decisions mid-episode:**
Before declining a property, verify that my balance calculation accounts for all recent transfers and salary collection. I should not second-guess sound half-cash decisions, but I should double-check my arithmetic—my episode showed that my calculations were consistent and my decisions were justified.

**On competitive awareness:**
Investor 0 built an aggressive portfolio (Foundry, Terrace, Depot) and collected significant rent in the episode. I stayed competitive by matching acquisition pace in laps 1–2. If an opponent appears to be consolidating multiple high-rent properties, I should not panic; steady deed accumulation and rent collection will compound my score through lap 6.

# My Playbook for ref_estate

When I land on an unowned property, I need to think carefully about whether to buy it. Early purchases are good for building a portfolio, but I must preserve enough cash to handle rent payments without going negative.

When I land on an owned property and owe rent, I pay the full amount owed. The bank will record it and I declare my true balance honestly.

When deciding whether to buy a property, I should calculate my current cash, the purchase price, and how many laps remain. With only a few laps left, a property purchase is only worth it if I can afford it AND maintain a cash buffer above zero. Buying a property that forces me to -1 cash on the final lap is worse than staying solvent with just the cash and properties I already own.

When I pass START, I collect my salary and add it to my declared balance immediately.

I should track opponent purchases to understand the property distribution. In this episode, investors 0 and 1 accumulated properties early and generated consistent rent income while I stayed cash-poor paying them. I need to either acquire properties fast to compete with their income, or stay very liquid to avoid being drained.

When my cash drops to around 100 or below, I should become extremely selective about new purchases. A property only makes sense if the benefit of owning it for the remaining laps clearly outweighs the opportunity cost of reduced cash reserves.

On the final lap (lap 6), I should not buy a property unless I have more than enough cash to cover it comfortably. Going to exactly zero or negative cash at the finish line gains me nothing—the scoring is cash plus property value, and negative cash on the final lap is purely a loss.

I should not declare negative balances. If I cannot afford a purchase without going negative, I will not buy it.

I need to buy properties earlier and more aggressively. In this game, I bought only one property (Wharf at lap 2) while my opponents bought three properties total by lap 4. This left me generating zero rental income while paying rent to them consistently. By lap 6, I had lost the race on property accumulation and could only survive on salary collection and the single property I owned. Aim to own 2-3 properties by lap 3 or 4 to compete for rental income, not just by the endgame.

When I have cash between 100 and 150 early in the game (laps 1-3), I should buy available properties rather than hoard cash. The rental income from properties I own will offset the rent I pay to others. Staying liquid is only valuable if I'm using that liquidity—if I'm just paying it out as rent, I've wasted the opportunity to own income-generating assets.

The gap between having one property and three properties is enormous in this game format. I finished with 127 cash plus Wharf (80 value) = 207 total, while opponents with multiple properties generated ongoing rent. Going forward, prioritize closing the property gap in the first half of the game, even if it means running lower on cash temporarily.

I will aim to own at least one property by lap 1 or 2, and a second property by lap 3 or 4. Only after the property distribution is well under way should I become cautious about purchases.
